outputs.L1: He walked to the window and gazed down twenty stories to the street—gaseous and dizzying as a swamp, invisible at this height, yet he knew it was there. A street lay below, and he knew it. It came with the apartment: the guarded foyers and halls, the doorman holstered beneath his uniform, the television split-screening the front and rear entrances. He knew it was all there, and that he was here, twenty stories above the unsettled swamp-mist. He knew the trucks bound for the bridge were still passing nearby—he could feel them rumbling in the soles of his feet—and so he knew the floor he walked upon was someone else's ceiling. Tonight it was all normal and countable: a two-year lease, for a desirable unit with a full view of the river, a five-by-three balcony beyond the door, a two-hundred-dollar deposit, fully carpeted, a self-defrosting refrigerator. The balcony door was stuck, but he could stare twenty stories down from the windowsill, watching the swamp-smokes curl and thin, watching the swamp lapping at the base, and the unpaid-for miracle receding one inch at a time.
outputs.L2: Crossing to the window, he gazed down twenty floors toward the street—murky and swirling like a marsh, invisible from this elevation, though he understood a street existed somewhere below. It had come bundled with the apartment: the protected lobbies and corridors, the doorman with a weapon concealed under his uniform, the television that divided its screen between the building's front and rear doors. He was certain all of it remained in place while he stood up here, twenty floors over the restless marsh-vapor. He was aware that the trucks heading toward the bridge continued to roll by nearby—he could sense their vibrations traveling up through his feet—so he understood that his floor served as another person's ceiling, and that everything felt ordinary and orderly this evening. A lease running two years, because this was a sought-after unit boasting a complete river view—a balcony measuring five by three feet accessible through the door for a $200 deposit, wall-to-wall carpeting throughout, a refrigerator that defrosted on its own—though the balcony door refused to budge. Still, he could peer twenty floors below from where he perched on the windowsill, observing the marsh-fumes twisting and dissolving, the swamp lapping against the foundation, the unpurchased marvel rising inch by inch.
outputs.L3:
From twenty stories up, the narrator peers down at a street he cannot see. Below him, the pavement dissolves into a swamp-like, gaseous mist that swallows the ground entirely, leaving only a hazy suggestion of the world beneath his window.

He knows the building is secure. The foyers are guarded, a doorman stands watch, and television cameras keep their electronic eyes trained on every entrance. These are the assurances of safety, the features designed to keep the outside world at a comfortable distance.

Yet the outside world makes itself felt in other ways. He can feel the trucks before he can imagine them—the heavy vibration of vehicles rumbling toward the bridge, their passage traveling up through the structure and into the soles of his feet, a persistent tremor in the floor beneath him.

The apartment came with its own particular arithmetic: a two-year lease, a river view, a balcony, a deposit, carpeting. Each detail is a line item, the ordinary vocabulary of renting a place to live, as though the terms themselves might anchor him to something solid and definite.

But the balcony door is stuck, sealing him inside. So he stands and watches the swamp mist instead, and lets his mind drift toward a slower, stranger vision—the water rising by degrees, creeping upward, patiently laying siege to the very base of the building where he lives.
outputs.L4:
The man stood at the window of his twentieth-floor apartment, forehead nearly touching the cool glass, staring down at a street that had vanished beneath a low, swamp-like mist. It gathered in the spaces between buildings and pooled over the pavement, gray-green and slow-moving, swallowing the parked cars and the sidewalk and the lamplight until there was nothing left of the city he knew—only this soft, breathing fog that seemed to belong to some older, wetter world.

He kept his hands in his pockets and let his mind wander through the small, orderly facts of his life, the way one might count coins to keep from thinking of something larger. The building was secure. There was a doorman in the lobby until eleven each night, and after that a keypad and a camera above the entrance, its little red light blinking with dependable indifference. His unit had two deadbolts. The windows were sealed and double-paned. The lease ran twenty-four months, with an option to renew, and he had signed it in blue ink at a folding table in the leasing office, initialing each page where the woman's manicured finger tapped. First month, last month, a security deposit held against damages. Pets under twenty pounds with prior approval. Quiet hours after ten.

These were the things he knew. These were the things that were true.

The balcony door, though, had never opened properly. It stuck in its track, warped or swollen or simply built wrong, and he had given up on it weeks ago. Now he watched through its smudged pane as the mist below did something it should not have been able to do.

It was rising.

Not quickly. Nothing so dramatic as that. But the level of it had crept upward while he stood there, climbing the face of the building floor by floor, and he understood with a strange, sinking certainty that it was coming for him. It moved with the patience of water finding its level, and he was simply another thing in its path, no more permanent than the cars it had already erased.

He thought, absurdly, of the lease again. Twenty-four months. As if that meant anything. As if the paper in his desk drawer could hold back what was climbing toward him now. He did not own this apartment. He did not own the glass, or the deadbolts, or the twenty floors of air beneath his feet. He had paid to borrow it, month by month, and even that borrowing felt suddenly provisional—a courtesy that could be withdrawn. Everything he stood on, everything that held him up here above the swamp, was unpaid-for in the deepest sense. Rented. Temporary. On loan from something that would, eventually, ask for it back.

The mist reached the tenth floor. The twelfth.

He did not move from the window. He watched it come, cataloging as it rose the exact and useless details of a life he had never truly owned, and he waited to see whether the sealed glass would hold.
outputs.L5:
# He Walked To

He walked to the edge of the pier where the morning fog still clung to the water. The wooden planks creaked beneath his boots, each step echoing in the silent dawn. He had made this journey countless times before, but today felt different somehow.

He walked to escape the noise of the city, to find a moment of quiet in a world that never seemed to stop moving. The salt air filled his lungs as he paused to watch a lone fishing boat drift toward the horizon.

He walked to the small café on the corner, the one with the flickering neon sign and the coffee that tasted like burnt memories. The bell above the door announced his arrival, and the familiar waitress nodded without a word. He walked to his usual table by the window and sat down, watching strangers pass by on the wet sidewalk outside.

Sometimes, he walked to think. Other times, he walked simply to feel his legs carry him somewhere—anywhere—away from the stillness of his empty apartment. The rhythm of walking gave him a strange comfort, a reminder that he was still moving forward even when everything else in his life seemed frozen in place.

He walked to the old bookstore, to the park bench beneath the oak tree, to the bridge where he had once made a promise he could no longer keep. Each destination held a fragment of who he used to be.

And when the day finally ended, he walked home—slower now, tired but somehow lighter, ready to do it all again tomorrow.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness passage in the style of Don DeLillo about a man alone in a high-rise apartment at night, looking out the window at a city that feels unreal and swamp-like below him.
counterfactuals.output:
The glass held him at a distance from himself. He stood there, forehead nearly touching, and the city went on breathing below in its wet electric way, a thing half-drowned, a swamp of light where the towers grew like something rooted in black water. He thought about the word city and how it had stopped meaning anything, the way a word does when you say it too many times, city, city, until it's just a sound the mouth makes, a small animal noise.

Down there the traffic moved in slow luminous strings and he could not hear it. That was the thing about height. It took the sound away and left you with the seeing, only the seeing, and the seeing became suspect after a while. Was it real. Were those cars. He knew they were cars the way you know a fact you've been told, secondhand, the knowledge of an absent thing.

The apartment hummed. Refrigerator, ventilation, the low tidal machinery of the building keeping him alive up here in the sky. He had signed papers for this. There had been a broker, a woman with very white teeth, and she had used the word views as though it were a possession you could hold. Now he possessed the views. He owned this drowned and glittering distance.

Somewhere a helicopter crossed, a red light pulsing, moving over the swamp of the grid. He watched it go. He thought, this is what it means to be modern, to stand behind sealed glass at night and feel the whole lit world become an idea of itself, unreal, a rumor of a place, mist rising off the avenues like heat off a marsh, and the man alone, the man watching, the man made almost weightless by the height and the hour and the terrible clarity of not being part of any of it.

He pressed his palm to the glass. It was cool. The city did not respond.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, dreamlike literary vignette where a character in a rented high-rise feels disconnected from the world below, blending real estate ad language into his paranoid interior monologue.
counterfactuals.output:
# Panoramic Views, Priced to Move

The unit came *fully furnished, move-in ready*, which meant someone else's absence had been staged as comfort. Desmond stood at the *floor-to-ceiling windows* and watched the city breathe without him, forty-one stories down, where the people moved like something spilled.

*An entertainer's dream.* But he entertained no one. The open-concept living space opened onto nothing but his own reflection, doubled in the glass, then tripled, a man receding into the amenity of himself.

Down there, the traffic pulsed in *sought-after locations*. Up here, the silence had a *premium finish*.

He hadn't signed a lease so much as agreed to a disappearance. *Discerning buyers will appreciate the privacy.* Yes. The privacy appreciated him back, watching, accruing. Nobody knew his name at this elevation. Nobody could reach the *secured entry, controlled access, twenty-four-hour concierge* who nodded without ever meeting his eye, as though Desmond were a package he'd been instructed not to open.

The clouds arrived at the window like tenants. They wanted in. He understood.

*Wake up to breathtaking sunrises.* He had stopped sleeping to be sure he wouldn't miss the moment the light came for him, red and clinical, sliding across the *engineered hardwood* like something looking for a drain. The building hummed. Everything here was *low-maintenance*, meaning it needed nothing from him, meaning he was the only thing in the unit that could rot.

He pressed his palm to the glass. Warm. As if the city had a fever, or he did, the two of them sharing symptoms across the unbridgeable *airspace*.

*Investment opportunity.* He was the investment. He was being held, appreciating, in a portfolio he couldn't name, by a landlord who existed only as a routing number and a smell of fresh paint that never quite dried.

Somewhere below, a siren threaded through the streets, mourning something. Up here it arrived softened, *thoughtfully appointed*, a grief with all the *modern conveniences*. He could not tell if it was coming for the city or coming for him, forty-one floors of nobody between the sound and his skin.

The listing had promised he would *feel right at home*.

He had. That was the terror of it. He had.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a piece of postmodern fiction: a lonely man in a guarded luxury apartment building, the street below imagined as a smoking swamp, obsessing over deposits and carpeting and a stuck balcony door.
counterfactuals.output:
**Non-Refundable**

The carpeting is called "Alabaster," though the invoice—which he has read forty times, which he reads now, again, holding it to the light as if it were a document of provenance—describes it as "Bone." He suspects the discrepancy is deliberate. He suspects everything is deliberate. Somewhere in a temperature-controlled office a man named Todd decided that "Bone" tested poorly and "Alabaster" tested well, and this man named Todd, who has never seen the carpet, who does not live here, who does not live *anywhere* in the sense that Marcus means it, now owns a portion of Marcus's security deposit that will never be returned.

He knows it will never be returned. That is the thing about deposits. They are not deposits. They are the fee for the privilege of believing, briefly, that you might get something back.

Below the window—forty-one floors below, past the doorman named Enrique who is not named Enrique, past the second doorman who guards the doorman—the street is a smoking swamp. He means this. He does not mean this metaphorically, or he means it exactly as metaphorically as anything means anything. Steam rises from the manholes in the industrial dawn. The taxis move through it like slow amphibians. A man in a wet coat submerges into a subway entrance and does not resurface. The whole city is drowning very slowly and calling it *weather.*

Up here it is clean. Up here it is Alabaster.

The balcony door is stuck.

He has not been able to open the balcony door in eleven days. He has documented this. He has photographed the track, the little rubber gasket, the point where the frame has swelled or the building has settled or the earth has shifted infinitesimally on its axis to trap him behind glass. He has emailed the management company. The management company has a portal. The portal generated a ticket. The ticket has a number, and the number has a status, and the status is "In Progress," which is the status of everything, which is the status of Marcus himself, forty-one years old, "In Progress," a ticket that will never resolve.

He does not need the balcony. He wants to be clear about this, with himself, at four in the morning, in his Alabaster living room. He does not go on the balcony. In three years he has stood on it perhaps six times, each time regretting the wind, the vertigo, the sense that the smoking swamp below wanted him. He does not want the balcony *open*. He wants the balcony *openable*. He wants the option. He is paying, he has calculated, roughly nine hundred dollars a month for options he does not exercise: the gym he does not visit, the rooftop pool that is drained in a season that is always about to end, the "resident lounge" where he has seen exactly one other resident, a woman who nodded at him with the sympathy of a fellow hostage.

The concierge desk downstairs has fresh flowers. This is important. This is where the money goes: fresh flowers no one smells, a marble no one sits on, a fountain in the lobby that produces a sound engineered to lower his heart rate as he passes it, defeated, twice a day. Security is very tight. He is guarded. He has never felt in danger and he has never felt safe. He is protected from a threat that is only ever the absence of threat. The building keeps out the swamp and in doing so it keeps out the world, and Marcus, who wanted this, who signed for this, who *paid the deposit*, sits inside the safety like a specimen in a jar labeled "Alabaster (formerly Bone)."

He calls the after-hours emergency line about the door. He knows it is not an emergency. He wants to say the word *emergency* to a human being.

A woman answers. She has a script. He can hear the script.

"I understand your concern about the balcony access," she says.

"It won't open."

"I've noted that the door won't open."

"I might need it," he says, and hears how it sounds, and does not stop. "In a fire. In a—I might need to get out."

A pause. The script does not cover this. Then, warmly, terribly, the script recovers:

"Your safety is our top priority."

And Marcus, holding the phone, looking at his own reflection floating forty-one stories above a city dissolving into steam, sealed inside the priority of his safety, feels the deposit inside him—the thing he put down long ago in exchange for a life he was promised he could get back—settle permanently, non-refundably, into someone else's account.

"Is there anything else I can help you with tonight?"

Below, the swamp exhales. A taxi surfaces, gulps a passenger, sinks.

"No," he says. "Everything's fine. Everything's Alabaster."

She does not know what this means. Neither, anymore, does he. He hangs up. He tries the door again. It holds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an unbroken run-on paragraph capturing urban alienation—a man at a window twenty floors up, trucks rumbling toward a bridge, the mist below like a swamp, and fragments of an apartment listing woven through his thoughts.
counterfactuals.output: He stands at the window twenty floors up with his forehead not quite touching the cold glass and below him the trucks are already moving in that gray before-dawn hour rumbling low and heavy toward the bridge whose lights hang suspended in nothing, spacious 1BR with abundant natural light, and the mist has come up off the river again pooling in the streets so the whole city looks drowned, looks like the swamp his grandfather described from some country he can no longer name, convenient access to transit and dining, and he thinks about how the trucks never stop, how someone somewhere is always hauling something toward somewhere else while he stands here doing nothing being no one, hardwood floors throughout, and the glass is the only thing between him and all that empty air and he presses his palm flat against it feeling the vibration of the diesel engines climbing the ramp, must see to appreciate, and down in the mist he can just make out the shapes of people small as insects hurrying with their collars up though he cannot hear them and they cannot see him and this is the arrangement, this is what it is, quiet building with responsive management, quiet because no one speaks, because he has lived here eight months and knows not a single name, not the woman across the hall nor the man who coughs through the wall at night, close to everything, close to everything and near to nothing, and the mist keeps rising and the trucks keep coming and the bridge keeps taking them and he stays, no pets, no smoking, no guarantors accepted, he stays at the glass watching the swamp of the world exhale its gray breath upward toward him as if it wanted him, available immediately, as if it had been waiting all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
